title: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
summary: Design cloud estates that survive one stolen credential: landing zones, SCPs, RCPs and data perimeters, Azure and Google guardrails, IAM escalation paths, confused deputies, serverless and workforce access.
outcomes: Design an AWS landing zone whose accounts, OUs and locked backups contain the blast radius of one stolen credential
Predict how SCPs combine down an organization tree and write deny-list guardrails with tested exemptions
Build a data perimeter with RCPs, SCPs and endpoint policies, and map it to Azure Policy and Google organization policy
Classify IAM privilege escalation paths, find them with graph tools and remove the cheapest edge
Explain the confused deputy and fix cross-account and cross-service trust with external IDs and source conditions
Secure serverless functions against event injection, over-broad execution roles and secrets in configuration
Replace long-lived human credentials with Identity Center, phishing-resistant MFA, PIM and tested break-glass access
Trace equivalent escalation routes in Azure and Google Cloud and prioritise CNAPP findings by attack path

lessons.title: Code Spaces 2014: why one account is one blast radius

blocks.md:
On Tuesday 17 June 2014, Code Spaces, a company that hosted Git and Subversion code repositories for its customers on AWS, came under a DDoS attack (distributed denial of service: many machines flooding a server at once). The company said this happened often and was normally handled quietly. This time, someone also had access to its Amazon EC2 control panel and left messages asking to be contacted. The contact turned into an extortion demand: pay a large fee and the attack stops.

When staff changed passwords to take the panel back, the intruder "had already created a number of backup logins to the panel" and began deleting things. By the time Code Spaces regained control, in the company's words, the intruder had "removed all EBS snapshots, S3 buckets, all AMI's, some EBS instances and several machine instances".

Three of those names need a gloss. **EBS** (Elastic Block Store) volumes are the virtual disks attached to EC2 servers, and an **EBS snapshot** is a point-in-time copy of one, the usual way to back them up. An **AMI** (Amazon Machine Image) is the template a server is launched from.

The company's summary: "most of our data, backups, machine configurations and offsite backups were either partially or completely deleted", over about 12 hours. Its statement ended by saying Code Spaces would not be able to operate beyond that point and would cease trading.

The intruder never needed to break into a single server: the company said no machine access had been achieved. One console login was enough, because the production data and every copy of it sat behind the same login, in one AWS account.

blocks.title: One login, one account, every copy of the data

scenes.caption: Code Spaces kept servers, disks, snapshots, images and backups in one AWS account. Every one of them is managed through the same control plane.
The intruder holds a console login. Before staff react, they create extra logins, so changing one password does not lock them out.
Deletion is an ordinary API call. Snapshots, buckets, images and instances go in the same session, because one identity could reach all of them.
The redesign: copies go to a separate backup account into a locked vault. The workload account can send copies but holds no identity that can delete them.
The same stolen login now fails at the backup account: it is not an identity there, and a compliance-mode lock refuses early deletion even to that account's root user.

blocks.md:
**Blast radius** is engineers' name for this: how far the damage from one failure or one stolen credential can spread. In the Code Spaces design, the blast radius of one console login was the whole company.

Cloud security architecture is the discipline of deciding, before anything goes wrong, where those radii end. You already know the parts from the cloud security and IAM course: accounts, policies, roles and logs. This course is about arranging them so that the failure of any single part is survivable. It asks three questions, and the lessons follow them:

1. **Where are the walls?** Accounts and organizations (lessons 1 and 2).
2. **What can nobody do, even an administrator?** Guardrails: SCPs, RCPs, data perimeters, Azure Policy and Google organization policies (lessons 3 to 5).
3. **Who can become whom?** Privilege escalation paths, cross-account trust, serverless functions and human access (lessons 6 to 10), then Azure and Google Cloud in depth and posture tooling (lessons 11 to 13).

Design as if any one credential will be stolen tomorrow. The test of an architecture is not "can an attacker get in?" but "what can one stolen login destroy or read?" Keep the data and its last good copy behind different identities, in different accounts.

**What the fix looks like today.** AWS Backup can copy backups into a vault in a different account (cross-account backup). On top of that, **AWS Backup Vault Lock** gives a vault **WORM** storage (write-once, read-many: data can be added but not changed or removed). In AWS's words, in a locked vault, "if any user (including the root user) attempts to delete a backup or change the lifecycle properties", AWS Backup denies the operation.

Vault Lock has two modes. In **governance mode**, users with enough IAM permissions can remove the lock. In **compliance mode**, there is a cooling-off period (AWS enforces at least 72 hours), and once the lock date passes, the vault and its lock "cannot be changed or deleted by any user or by AWS"; backups stay until their retention ends. That is exactly the property Code Spaces lacked: a copy that no login, however powerful, can delete early.

blocks.code:
# Run in the BACKUP account, not the workload account.
# Lock the vault in compliance mode: changeable for 3 days, then immutable.
aws backup put-backup-vault-lock-configuration \
    --backup-vault-name org-backups \
    --min-retention-days 35 \
    --max-retention-days 365 \
    --changeable-for-days 3
blocks.caption: Setting --changeable-for-days is what puts the lock in compliance mode; AWS requires 3 or more because of the 72-hour cooling-off period. Test retention values first: after the lock date they cannot be changed.

blocks.md:
**Defender view.**

- *Prevent:* MFA on every console login, no long-lived administrator keys, workloads and backups in separate accounts, a compliance-mode vault for the last good copy.
- *Detect:* in CloudTrail (the AWS audit log), watch for new users and login profiles (`CreateUser`, `CreateLoginProfile`, `CreateAccessKey`) followed by bursts of destructive calls such as `DeleteSnapshot`, `DeleteBucket` or `DeregisterImage`. The Code Spaces intruder's first move, creating backup logins, is exactly the persistence pattern from the leaked-key response lesson of the cloud security and IAM course.
- *Respond:* contain from an identity the attacker cannot reach (a break-glass role in another account, lesson 10), and restore from the vault they cannot touch.

blocks.question: Which single change would most likely have preserved Code Spaces' customer data?
options: Copies of backups in a separate account, in a vault locked in compliance mode
Stronger DDoS protection in front of the servers
More EC2 instances spread across Regions in the same account
Changing the console password faster once the intruder was noticed
blocks.explain: The loss came from one identity being able to delete everything, including backups. A copy in another account, locked against early deletion, survives any login in the workload account. Regions in the same account are reachable by the same account's logins; faster password changes failed because the intruder had already made extra logins.

blocks.question: A backup vault is locked in compliance mode and its lock date has passed. An administrator signed in as that account's root user tries to delete a backup that is still inside its retention period. What happens?
options: The deletion succeeds, because root bypasses all IAM policy
The deletion succeeds only if MFA is used
AWS Backup denies it; not even the root user or AWS can remove the lock or delete early
The deletion is queued until the 72-hour cooling-off period ends
blocks.explain: AWS's documentation says AWS Backup denies deletion attempts by any user, including the root user, and that after the grace time a compliance-mode lock cannot be changed or deleted by any user or by AWS. The 72-hour cooling-off happens before the lock date, not after.

lessons.title: Landing zones: an account layout that contains failure

blocks.md:
Picture a 40-person company that has run everything in one AWS account for three years. The new security engineer is asked to "fix the account structure". Where do the logs go? Which account runs the security tools? Where do developers experiment? Who may touch the account that pays the bill?

The answer has a name. The documentation of AWS Control Tower (AWS's service for setting up and governing a multi-account environment) defines a **landing zone** as "a well-architected, multi-account environment that's based on security and compliance best practices": the container that holds all your organizational units (OUs, folders of accounts), accounts, users and resources. Recall from the cloud security and IAM course that **AWS Organizations** groups accounts under one management account and that SCPs attach to OUs. A landing zone is the decision about which OUs and accounts to create, and what each may do.

AWS's whitepaper *Organizing Your AWS Environment Using Multiple Accounts* recommends a set of OUs and says you might not need all of them at first:

- **Foundational OUs**, owned by a central platform team: the **Security OU** and the **Infrastructure OU** (shared networking and other common services).
- **Workloads OU**: the business applications, usually split into production and non-production.
- **Sandbox OU**: experimentation, with limited access to internal networks.
- **Procedural OUs**, such as **Suspended** (accounts frozen for security or policy reasons), **Policy Staging** (to test new organization policies before they spread), Exceptions, Transitional and Deployments.

The whitepaper's reasoning is blast radius again: the isolation of an account means a misconfiguration or malicious activity in one account "can be contained and prevented from impacting workloads in other accounts".

Two accounts in the Security OU do most of the security work (AWS Control Tower created both automatically up to landing zone version 3.3; version 4.0 lets you define your own structure):

- **Log Archive**: "a consolidation point for log data" from every account: CloudTrail API logs, change records from AWS Config (the service that records every configuration change) and other security-relevant logs. Teams in each account read their own logs short term; the authoritative copy lives here, where workload administrators cannot delete it.
- **Security Tooling** (also called **Audit**): the home of the security services. The organization makes this account the **delegated administrator** (a member account allowed to run a service for the whole organization) for Security Hub CSPM (posture checks), GuardDuty (threat detection), Macie (finds sensitive data in S3), Inspector (vulnerability scanning), Detective (investigation) and IAM Access Analyzer, so findings from every account arrive here, and it gets view-only access into all accounts for investigations.

blocks.title: A small landing zone, and where failure stops

scenes.caption: The organization root has four OUs. Each account is its own security boundary; the management account sits beside the tree, not inside an OU.
Every account sends CloudTrail and Config logs to Log Archive. Workload administrators can write logs there but cannot delete the archive.
A developer's key in the Sandbox is stolen. The thief controls one experimental account; Prod, Network and the logs are other accounts with no trust toward it.
The management account is the exception: SCPs do not restrict its users and roles. Keep it empty of workloads and give very few people access.

blocks.md:
**The management account is special, so keep it boring.** AWS Organizations' best practices say to use it "only for tasks that require the management account", to avoid deploying workloads there, and to limit access to the few admins who change the organization. The reason is stated plainly: SCPs "do not work to restrict any users or roles in the management account". Control Tower's documentation says the same about its controls: the root user and administrators in the management account "can perform work that controls would otherwise deny", on purpose, so the account can never lock itself out.

So the most powerful account is also the one your guardrails cannot reach. Delegated administration exists to keep daily work out of it: security tools run from Security Tooling, not from the management account.

blocks.code:
# From the management account: build the OU skeleton once
aws organizations create-organizational-unit --parent-id r-a1b2 --name Security
aws organizations create-organizational-unit --parent-id r-a1b2 --name Workloads
aws organizations create-organizational-unit --parent-id r-a1b2 --name Sandbox

# Make the Security Tooling account (here 222233334444) the GuardDuty
# administrator for the whole organization, so findings land there
aws guardduty enable-organization-admin-account --admin-account-id 222233334444
blocks.caption: IDs are placeholders. In practice teams create this skeleton with AWS Control Tower or infrastructure as code rather than by hand, so the layout itself is reviewed and versioned.

blocks.md:
**The other clouds use the same shape.** Microsoft's Cloud Adoption Framework describes an **Azure landing zone** as two parts: a **platform landing zone** ("the centralized foundation that establishes governance, security, and shared resources") and **workload landing zones** where application teams deploy "within the guardrails of the platform landing zone". Its reference architecture puts security and management, identity and connectivity in their own subscriptions, under management groups (you met management groups and subscriptions in the cloud security and IAM course).

In **Google Cloud** the organization resource sits on top, folders play the role of OUs, and projects are the isolation unit. Organization policies set on a folder are inherited by every project below it, as lesson 5 shows.

Common mistake: "our security tooling runs in the management account because it can see everything there." That puts your most targeted tools in the one account no SCP protects. Delegate administration to a Security Tooling account and keep the management account for organization tasks only.

blocks.question: Where should the organization's authoritative CloudTrail logs be stored?
options: In each workload account, so its admins can manage them
In a Log Archive account in the Security OU, which workload administrators cannot change
In the management account, which SCPs cannot restrict
In the Sandbox account, where storage is cheapest
blocks.explain: AWS's whitepaper describes the Log Archive account as the consolidation point for every account's logs. Logs in the account they describe can be deleted by whoever compromises that account; the management account should hold no workloads or data.

blocks.question: A platform engineer wants to run a small automation Lambda in the management account because it already has broad permissions. What is the main security problem?
options: Lambda functions cannot run in a management account
The function would be billed twice
Delegated administrators would lose access to GuardDuty
SCPs do not restrict users and roles in the management account, so a bug or stolen credential there escapes every guardrail
blocks.explain: AWS's best practices keep workloads out of the management account precisely because SCPs do not apply to it. Anything running there with broad permissions is a path around every organization guardrail.

lessons.title: Service control policies in depth: inheritance and exemptions

blocks.md:
Think of an office tower with a guard at the street door, another at the floor lobby and a lock on each suite. To reach a suite you need a yes at every door on the way, and a single "no entry" sign at any door stops you. A **service control policy** (SCP: an organization policy that sets the most an account's users and roles may do) works the same way along the path from the organization root, through each OU, down to the account.

You met SCPs in the cloud security and IAM course as an upper limit that grants nothing. This lesson is about how several of them combine, how to write ones that do not break production, and how to exempt the few identities that must step over them.

AWS's evaluation rules for SCPs, from the Organizations user guide:

1. **An Allow is needed at every level.** For an action to be permitted in Account B, "a SCP that allows the permission or service should be attached to Root, the Production OU, and to Account B itself." A level with no matching Allow denies it.
2. **A Deny at any level wins** for everything beneath that level.
3. **FullAWSAccess** is an AWS managed SCP that allows everything; AWS attaches it to every root, OU and account when SCPs are enabled. If it is removed and nothing replaces it at some level, everything below that level is blocked.

This gives two strategies. A **deny list** keeps FullAWSAccess everywhere and adds Deny statements for what must never happen; AWS's published examples use this style. An **allow list** replaces FullAWSAccess with policies naming only the services you use, so new services stay off until approved, at the cost of more maintenance.

blocks.title: A simplified SCP evaluator walking one path

scenes.caption: The path has three levels. Root keeps FullAWSAccess; the Prod OU allows everything but denies creating IAM users; the account allows only S3 and IAM.
s3:GetObject: no Deny matches at any level, and each level has an Allow that matches (*, *, s3:*). It passes the SCPs.
iam:CreateUser: Root allows it, but the Prod OU has an explicit Deny. Every account in that OU is blocked, whatever the account-level SCP says.
scenes.output:
s3:GetObject       passes SCPs
iam:CreateUser     DENY (explicit deny at Prod OU)

scenes.caption: ec2:RunInstances: nothing denies it, but the account-level SCP allows only s3:* and iam:*. No Allow at that level means deny.
scenes.output:
s3:GetObject       passes SCPs
iam:CreateUser     DENY (explicit deny at Prod OU)
ec2:RunInstances   DENY (no allow at Account)

blocks.md: The evaluator is a teaching model, not AWS's code: real evaluation checks for explicit denies across all policies first, matches action names case-insensitively, evaluates conditions, and only then combines the result with identity and resource policies. Passing the SCPs only means the action is not ruled out; something must still grant it.

blocks.prompt: A team attaches an SCP to the organization root that contains only a Deny for `organizations:LeaveOrganization`, and in the same change detaches FullAWSAccess from the root to "keep things tidy". What happens to the member accounts?
blocks.reveal: Everything stops. AWS's documentation walks through exactly this case: when the root has only a Deny statement and no Allow, member accounts lose all access, because SCPs need an explicit Allow at every level in the path. A deny-only SCP must sit alongside FullAWSAccess (or another Allow), never replace it. This is why AWS recommends testing SCPs in a separate OU first.

blocks.md:
**Exemptions without a Principal element.** SCPs do not support `Principal` or `NotPrincipal`; they apply to every user and role in the affected accounts. To let one platform role step over a guardrail, put the exemption in a condition on the global key `aws:PrincipalArn` (the ARN of the role or user making the call). AWS's own example SCPs do exactly this with an `ArnNotLike` test.

Common guardrails in AWS's published examples: deny actions outside approved Regions (with a list of global services left out), deny member accounts leaving the organization, deny changes to security services and logging, deny creating IAM users, access keys and login profiles, and deny changes to platform-owned roles. The second code block below protects the roles your platform team relies on, so an account administrator cannot edit them to escalate.

blocks.caption: Simplified from AWS's region-control example, which exempts a longer list of global services. NotAction means: deny every action except these. The two conditions are ANDed, so the break-glass role is never denied.
Simplified from AWS's example that denies modifications to specific IAM roles. Only the pipeline role may change, tag or assume roles named platform-*; an account administrator cannot.

blocks.md:
**Rolling out without breaking production.** AWS's examples come with a warning: do not attach SCPs "without thoroughly testing the impact", ideally first in a separate organization or a Policy Staging OU. Use the service last accessed data in IAM to see which services accounts actually use before writing an allow list.

**Defender view.** An SCP denial appears in the caller's error message: AWS documents the form "is not authorized to perform: codecommit:ListRepositories with an explicit deny in a service control policy", and "because no service control policy allows" for the implicit case. In CloudTrail these are failed calls with an AccessDenied error code. A burst of SCP denials from one role is worth a look: it is either a broken deployment or someone probing what the guardrails block.

SCPs combine by intersection down the tree: an Allow is needed at every level, and a Deny at any level wins. Prefer deny-list SCPs on top of FullAWSAccess, exempt only named platform or break-glass roles through `aws:PrincipalArn`, and test every change in a staging OU first.

blocks.question: The Root and the Workloads OU keep FullAWSAccess. The Test OU under Workloads has FullAWSAccess plus a Deny on `ec2:*`. Account D is in the Test OU and has FullAWSAccess attached directly. Can a role in Account D call `ec2:RunInstances` if its identity policy allows it?
options: Yes, because Account D's own SCP allows everything
Yes, because SCPs never apply to EC2
No, because the Deny attached to the Test OU applies to every account below it
No, because the role also needs an Allow in the management account
blocks.explain: This is AWS's layered-deny scenario: a Deny at any level of the path applies to all accounts beneath it, and an Allow lower down cannot override it.

blocks.question: You need every role in member accounts to be blocked from disabling GuardDuty, except the security team's automation role. Which SCP technique fits?
options: A Deny statement with an ArnNotLike condition on aws:PrincipalArn naming the automation role
A Deny with "Principal" set to everything except the automation role
Removing FullAWSAccess from the Security OU
An Allow statement listing only the automation role
blocks.explain: SCPs do not support Principal or NotPrincipal, so exemptions go in a condition on aws:PrincipalArn, which is how AWS's own example SCPs exempt privileged roles. An SCP Allow cannot name principals and grants nothing.

lessons.title: Resource control policies and the data perimeter

blocks.md:
SCPs limit what **your** identities can do. They say nothing about strangers. Suppose a developer in your Prod account writes a bucket policy that, by mistake, grants read access to an account outside your company. The stranger's request is checked against their own account's SCPs, not yours. Your SCPs never run.

A **resource control policy** (RCP) closes that gap. AWS introduced RCPs as the resource-side twin of SCPs: "Use an SCP when you need to limit permissions of IAM principals within your organization's member accounts. Use an RCP when you need to restrict IAM principals that are external to your organization accounts making requests to access resources within your organization's member accounts."

How RCPs behave, from the AWS Organizations guide:

- Like SCPs, an RCP **grants nothing**; effective access is the intersection of the RCPs, the SCPs and the identity or resource policies.
- An RCP applies to resources in member accounts **whoever** the caller is, including root users and principals from other organizations.
- You can only write `Deny` statements, with `"Principal": "*"`, and narrow them with conditions. An AWS managed policy, **RCPFullAWSAccess**, is attached everywhere and cannot be detached, so existing access keeps working until you add a Deny.
- RCPs do not apply to the management account's resources, to service-linked roles, or to AWS managed KMS keys.
- They cover a list of services that keeps growing, including S3, STS (so they can guard role trust), KMS, SQS and Secrets Manager.

**The data perimeter.** AWS describes a **data perimeter** as "a set of preventive controls" that help ensure "only your trusted identities access your trusted resources from expected networks". Three perimeters, each enforced from two sides:

- **Identity perimeter**: only trusted identities can access my resources (an RCP on resources), and only trusted identities are allowed from my network (VPC endpoint policies).
- **Resource perimeter**: my identities can access only trusted resources (an SCP using `aws:ResourceOrgID`), and only trusted resources can be reached from my network (VPC endpoint policies).
- **Network perimeter**: my identities can act only from expected networks (an SCP), and my resources can be accessed only from expected networks (an RCP).

"Trusted" is defined by you: principals and resources in your organization, plus AWS services acting for you and named partners. You built one piece of this in the cloud security and IAM course: the SCP that stopped stolen instance credentials working outside their VPC is a network perimeter control.

blocks.title: Which policy type enforces which perimeter (1 = default control)

scenes.caption: Rows are the three perimeters, columns the policy type that carries the control. Each perimeter is enforced from two sides; AWS's default examples follow this grid.
Identity perimeter: an RCP on your resources rejects callers from outside the organization, and VPC endpoint policies reject outside identities on your networks.
Resource perimeter: an SCP stops your identities using resources outside your organization (such as a stranger's bucket for exfiltration), backed by endpoint policies.
Network perimeter: an SCP limits where your identities may call from, and an RCP limits where your resources may be reached from.

blocks.caption: Simplified from AWS's identity_perimeter_rcp.json example. Deny when the caller is outside the organization AND is not the named partner account AND is not an AWS service principal. Keys inside one operator, and the operators themselves, are ANDed.

blocks.md:
Reading the conditions: `aws:PrincipalOrgID` is the organization ID of the calling principal; `aws:PrincipalAccount` lets one partner account through; `aws:PrincipalIsAWSService` is true when an AWS **service principal** (such as `cloudtrail.amazonaws.com` delivering logs to your bucket) makes the call. AWS's whitepaper notes that service principals are "not part of your AWS organization like IAM roles are", so without that exemption your own log delivery would break. The `IfExists` suffix means: if the key is present, run the test; if it is absent, count the condition as true. So a request that carries no principal organization at all, such as an anonymous one, still matches the Deny.

Two terms from the grid above: `aws:ResourceOrgID` is the organization of the account that owns the resource being called, and a VPC endpoint policy is a resource policy on an endpoint that limits who and what can be reached through it.

The sequence below follows three requests to a bucket whose policy has the developer's mistake in it.

blocks.title: A bucket policy mistake meets an identity perimeter RCP

scenes.caption: A stranger's account was granted s3:GetObject by a mistaken bucket policy. On its own, that policy would allow the read.
S3 includes the bucket owner's RCPs in the decision. The caller's PrincipalOrgID is not yours and it is not an AWS service, so the Deny matches.
The stranger gets a generic AccessDenied: S3 names the policy type only for callers in your own account or organization. The bucket policy is still wrong, but it can no longer leak data.
A role in your own organization makes the same call. Its PrincipalOrgID matches, the RCP does not apply, and normal policy evaluation decides.
CloudTrail's service principal delivers logs. aws:PrincipalIsAWSService is true, so the exemption keeps your logging working.

blocks.md: RCPs can break things you did not know depended on outside access: a partner's integration, a third-party monitoring tool, an AWS feature using a service principal. AWS "strongly recommends" not attaching RCPs to the root without testing; review IAM Access Analyzer's external access findings and CloudTrail AccessDenied errors first, then roll out OU by OU.

**Defender view.** Before writing an RCP, list what is shared today: IAM Access Analyzer's external access findings report each resource policy granting access to principals outside your zone of trust. After rollout, watch AccessDenied errors in CloudTrail (for S3 object reads this needs data event logging, which is off by default). Callers inside your organization see the text "with an explicit deny in a resource control policy"; outsiders get only a generic Access Denied, so search by error code and calling account, not by message. A spike of denials from an unknown account means the perimeter just stopped someone, and the resource policy that would have let them in still needs fixing.

blocks.question: A bucket policy in a member account grants read access to an account in a different organization. Which control stops that outside account reading objects, even though the bucket policy allows it?
options: An SCP attached to your organization root
A permissions boundary on the bucket owner's roles
Nothing: a resource policy that allows access always wins
An RCP denying access when aws:PrincipalOrgID is not your organization
blocks.explain: SCPs limit your own principals; the outsider's request is not subject to your SCPs. An RCP applies to resources in your member accounts whoever the caller is. Permissions boundaries limit identities, not resources.

blocks.question: An identity perimeter RCP omits the aws:PrincipalIsAWSService exemption. What is the most likely first symptom?
options: Root users in member accounts can no longer sign in
AWS services that use service principals, such as CloudTrail delivering logs to a bucket, start failing
The management account's buckets become public
Nothing changes, because RCPs do not apply to S3
blocks.explain: Service principals are not members of your organization, so a PrincipalOrgID test denies them unless exempted. AWS's whitepaper uses CloudTrail log delivery as the example. RCPs do not apply to the management account at all.

lessons.title: The same guardrails in Azure Policy and Google organization policy

blocks.md:
Recall the 2023 Microsoft AI research exposure from the cloud security and IAM course: a public GitHub README linked an **account SAS** token (shared access signature, a signed URL) that gave full control over a whole storage account and stayed valid until 2051. The token was signed with the storage account key. Azure RBAC (who may do what) never came into it: whoever held the URL had access.

So ask an architect's question: which organization-wide setting would have made that token useless, whatever any one researcher did? In Azure, rules about how resources may be **configured** belong to **Azure Policy**, the service that plays the guardrail role SCPs play in AWS.

How Azure Policy works, from Microsoft Learn:

- A **policy definition** is a rule written as `if` (conditions on resource properties) and `then` (an **effect**). An **initiative** groups definitions.
- An **assignment** applies a definition at a scope: a management group, subscription, resource group or single resource, inherited below it. Microsoft notes that even when the assignment sits on a management group, only resources at subscription or resource group level are evaluated.
- Effects include `audit` (record non-compliance), `deny` (reject the create or update), `modify` and `append` (change the request), `auditIfNotExists` and `deployIfNotExists` (check or deploy a related resource), `denyAction` and `disabled`.
- For a create or update, `disabled` is checked first, then `append` and `modify`, then `deny`; the `IfNotExists` effects run after the resource provider succeeds.
- When several assignments apply, Microsoft calls the result "cumulative most restrictive": any matching `deny` blocks the request.

blocks.caption: Simplified from the built-in definition "Storage accounts should prevent shared key access" (its effect parameter allows Audit, Deny or Disabled). The property is unset by default, and an unset value permits Shared Key, so the rule matches both missing and true.

blocks.md:
Why that one property matters for the Microsoft case: Microsoft's documentation says an account SAS or service SAS "is authorized with Shared Key and isn't permitted on a request to Blob Storage" when `AllowSharedKeyAccess` is false. A **user delegation SAS**, signed with Microsoft Entra credentials, still works, and it is the kind Microsoft recommends. With the policy assigned as Deny at a management group, nobody below it can create a storage account that accepts account SAS tokens for blobs. Accounts that already exist are only marked non-compliant, so they still need remediating.

A second guardrail limits lifetime. A **SAS expiration policy** on a storage account sets an upper limit on how long any SAS may be valid. Its default action, **Log**, allows out-of-policy tokens but records their use; the **Block** action denies them. A 2051 expiry under a one-day limit with Block set would simply be refused. Microsoft's own advice is to start with Audit or Log, find the applications still using Shared Key, move them to Entra authorization, then switch to Deny and Block.

blocks.title: A Deny assignment on shared key access, from creation to use

scenes.caption: A researcher creates a storage account and leaves Shared Key access on. The request goes through Azure Resource Manager, the API every Azure change passes through.
Azure Policy evaluates assignments inherited from the management group. The built-in rule matches and its effect is Deny.
Deny stops the request before it reaches the resource provider and returns 403 (Forbidden). Nothing was created, so there is nothing to clean up later.
The researcher sets AllowSharedKeyAccess to false and the account is created. Data is shared with a user delegation SAS signed through Entra ID.
Someone tries an old-style account SAS against Blob Storage. It depends on the account key, so the storage service refuses it.

blocks.md:
**Google Cloud: the Organization Policy Service.** Google's equivalent sets **constraints** on the organization, a folder or a project. A list constraint allows or denies a set of values (for example, which locations may hold resources); a boolean constraint is on or off. Google's docs: when a policy is set on a resource, "all descendants of that resource inherit the organization policy by default", and a descendant can override it only if the policy allows that. Changes can take up to 15 minutes to be enforced.

For organizations created on or after May 3, 2024, Google enforces a **security baseline** of constraints at creation, including:

- `iam.managed.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation` and `iam.disableServiceAccountKeyUpload`: no long-lived service account keys.
- `iam.automaticIamGrantsForDefaultServiceAccounts`: default service accounts do not get the broad Editor role.
- `iam.allowedPolicyMemberDomains`: only identities from your own organization or Workspace customer can be granted roles.
- `storage.uniformBucketLevelAccess`: no per-object ACLs on buckets.

blocks.code:
# policy.yaml: block service account key creation for the whole organization
name: organizations/123456789012/policies/iam.managed.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation
spec:
  rules:
  - enforce: true

# Apply it, then check what is actually in force
gcloud org-policies set-policy policy.yaml
gcloud org-policies describe iam.managed.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation \
    --organization=123456789012 --effective
blocks.caption: The format follows Google's boolean-constraint example. Older organizations, created before the baseline, need these set by hand; the effective view shows what a project really inherits.

blocks.md:
Two more Google controls complete the mapping:

- **IAM deny policies** let you write "deny rules that prevent certain principals from using certain permissions, regardless of the roles they're granted", and IAM checks them before allow policies. That is the closest Google equivalent to an SCP's Deny.
- **VPC Service Controls** draw a **service perimeter** around projects and services such as Cloud Storage and BigQuery. Google says the perimeter helps against "clients using stolen OAuth or service account credentials" and "prevents reading data from or copying data to a resource outside the perimeter": the same goals as AWS's data perimeter in lesson 4.

The rough mapping: AWS SCP and Google IAM deny policy limit what principals can do; AWS RCP and VPC endpoint policies, and Google VPC Service Controls, guard the data; Azure Policy and Google organization policy constrain how resources may be configured.

Identity rules (RBAC, IAM) say who may act. Configuration guardrails (Azure Policy, Google organization policy, AWS SCPs used as preventive controls) say what no one may build, such as storage that accepts account keys or service accounts with downloadable keys. Set them high in the hierarchy, start in audit mode, then deny.

blocks.question: Which single organization-wide setting would have made the Microsoft researchers' account SAS unusable for reading blobs?
options: Azure Policy denying storage accounts that allow Shared Key access, so AllowSharedKeyAccess is false
An Azure RBAC role assignment of Storage Blob Data Reader
A SAS expiration policy with the default Log action
Moving the storage account to a different region
blocks.explain: An account SAS is authorized with Shared Key, and Microsoft documents that it is not permitted on Blob requests when AllowSharedKeyAccess is false. RBAC does not govern SAS tokens; the Log action only records out-of-policy SAS use and still allows it.

blocks.question: A Google Cloud project owner wants to create a downloadable key for a service account. The organization was created in June 2024 and nobody has changed its policies. What happens?
options: The key is created, because project owners have every permission
The key is created but expires after 15 minutes
Creation is blocked by the baseline constraint disabling service account key creation, inherited from the organization
Only VPC Service Controls can block it
blocks.explain: Organizations created on or after May 3, 2024 get the security baseline, which includes iam.managed.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation. Organization policy constraints apply regardless of the IAM roles a project owner holds. The 15 minutes is how long policy changes can take to propagate.

blocks.question: In Azure, two policy assignments apply to the same subscription: one audits storage accounts that allow public network access, the other denies them. A new storage account with public access is submitted. What happens?
options: It is created and marked non-compliant, because audit runs first
It is denied: layered assignments are cumulative most restrictive
The newer assignment wins
Azure asks the creator to choose an effect
blocks.explain: Each assignment is evaluated independently and a matching deny blocks the request; Microsoft describes the result of layering as cumulative most restrictive. Deny is evaluated before audit for create and update requests.

lessons.title: IAM privilege escalation: the classes behind Rhino's 21 methods

blocks.md:
Start with Dana, a developer whose role cannot read the payroll bucket. Dana's role may, however, create a new version of the managed policy attached to it. A new version can say anything, including `"Action": "*"`. So Dana can read payroll, and everything else, after one API call.

That is **privilege escalation** in IAM: using the permissions you have to obtain permissions you were not meant to have. The cloud security and IAM course warned that IAM write actions are administrator rights in disguise. This lesson turns that warning into a map.

In 2018 Spencer Gietzen of Rhino Security Labs, a penetration testing company, published **21 AWS IAM privilege escalation methods**, "which allow an attacker to escalate from a compromised low-privilege account to full administrative privileges". The post credits earlier research by Asaf Hecht and the team at CyberArk, a privileged-access security company, on "AWS Shadow Admins": principals that are not called administrators but can make themselves one. It shipped with a scanner, aws_escalate.py, and previewed **Pacu**, Rhino's open source AWS exploitation framework, "aptly named after a type of Piranha in the Amazon".

Twenty-one methods are hard to remember. Five classes are not, and every method on the list belongs to one of them.

**1. Rewrite your own permissions.** `iam:CreatePolicyVersion` on a policy you hold: Rhino notes a flag sets the new version as default without needing `iam:SetDefaultPolicyVersion`. `iam:SetDefaultPolicyVersion` alone: roll back to an older, broader version still stored. `iam:AttachUserPolicy`, `AttachGroupPolicy`, `AttachRolePolicy`, the inline `iam:PutUserPolicy`, `PutGroupPolicy`, `PutRolePolicy`, and `iam:AddUserToGroup` on a more powerful group.

**2. Take over another principal's credentials.** `iam:CreateAccessKey` on another user (if they have fewer than two keys), `iam:CreateLoginProfile` (give a user a console password) and `iam:UpdateLoginProfile` (change it).

**3. Rewrite who may assume a role.** `iam:UpdateAssumeRolePolicy` plus `sts:AssumeRole`: edit a powerful role's trust policy to trust yourself, then assume it.

**4. Pass a powerful role to compute you control.** `iam:PassRole` lets you hand a role to an AWS service (the cloud security and IAM course introduced it). Combined with a way to run your code there, you borrow that role: `ec2:RunInstances` with an instance profile; `lambda:CreateFunction` plus `lambda:InvokeFunction`, or plus `lambda:CreateEventSourceMapping` so a stream from DynamoDB (AWS's NoSQL database) triggers it; `glue:CreateDevEndpoint` (AWS Glue, a data-processing service); `cloudformation:CreateStack` (CloudFormation, AWS's infrastructure-as-code service); and AWS Data Pipeline (a data-movement service, now closed to new customers).

**5. Change what already runs as a role.** `lambda:UpdateFunctionCode` on a function with a powerful execution role, or `glue:UpdateDevEndpoint` to add your SSH key to an existing Glue endpoint. Nothing new is created, which makes this class quieter.

AWS states the principle behind class 4 in its PassRole documentation: make sure "a user doesn't pass a role where the role has more permissions than you want the user to have".

blocks.title: Five ways a narrow principal becomes an administrator

scenes.caption: A principal with a narrow-looking policy. Each box on the right is a class of escalation; any one edge reaching Admin is enough.
Class 1: the principal edits its own policies (new policy version, older version, attach or put a policy, join a group). The change applies to itself immediately.
Class 2: it creates a key or console password for a more powerful user, then signs in as that user.
Class 3: it edits a powerful role's trust policy to trust itself, then assumes the role.
Class 4: it passes an existing powerful role to new compute (EC2, Lambda, Glue, CloudFormation) and runs its own code there with that role.
Class 5: it changes the code or keys of compute that already runs as a powerful role, and waits for the next invocation.
The defence cuts edges, not boxes: scope PassRole and IAM writes by resource, require permissions boundaries, and deny edits to platform roles with an SCP.

blocks.prompt: A user's only IAM permission is `iam:CreatePolicyVersion` on the one customer managed policy attached to that user. Is this user an administrator?
blocks.reveal: Effectively, yes. Rhino's method 1: the user writes a new version of their own policy granting any action on any resource, and sets it as the default in the same call, without needing `iam:SetDefaultPolicyVersion`. One narrow-sounding permission on the wrong resource is full control. A scanner that only looks for `AdministratorAccess` would miss it, which is why the next lesson treats permissions as a graph.

blocks.caption: VULNERABLE: a developer policy that looks like routine Lambda work. PassRole on any role plus CreateFunction and InvokeFunction is Rhino's method 15; CreatePolicyVersion on any policy is method 1.
FIXED: PassRole only for app-lambda-* roles and only to Lambda; functions only named app-*; new roles only with the app-boundary permissions boundary attached. CreatePolicyVersion is gone.

blocks.md:
**Why the fix works.** Each statement removes a class 4 or class 1 edge. `iam:PassedToService` (a condition key that "applies to only the PassRole action") stops the developer handing app roles to EC2 or CloudFormation. The `Resource` on PassRole means the powerful platform roles cannot be passed at all. The `iam:PermissionsBoundary` condition means any role the developer creates or edits carries the boundary, so its effective permissions can never exceed `app-boundary`, however broad its own policy. Protect the boundary policy itself (the developer must not be able to edit it or remove it from a role), add the lesson 3 SCP that protects `platform-*` roles, and class 3 edits on them are denied too.

Rhino's own top recommendation is the same idea: fully use the `Resource` element, including policy variables such as `${aws:username}`, so self-service actions like creating access keys or a login profile apply only to the caller.

**Defender view.**

- *Detect:* every method is a control plane call, so CloudTrail records it. Alert on `CreatePolicyVersion`, `SetDefaultPolicyVersion`, `Attach*Policy`, `Put*Policy`, `AddUserToGroup`, `CreateAccessKey` and `CreateLoginProfile` for another user, `UpdateAssumeRolePolicy`, and `UpdateFunctionCode` outside your pipeline. GuardDuty raises `PrivilegeEscalation:IAMUser/AnomalousBehavior` (default severity Medium) when "an API commonly used to obtain high-level permissions" is invoked in an anomalous way.
- *Prevent:* resource-scoped IAM writes, PassRole with `iam:PassedToService`, permissions boundaries for delegated role creation, SCPs protecting platform roles and denying IAM users and keys.
- *Respond:* treat the escalated principal and everything it could reach as compromised; revert policy versions and trust policies, and remove new keys, login profiles and functions.

blocks.question: A role has `iam:PassRole` on `*`, `lambda:CreateFunction` and `lambda:CreateEventSourceMapping`, but not `lambda:InvokeFunction`. Is there an escalation path?
options: No, because without InvokeFunction the function can never run
Only if the role also has iam:AttachRolePolicy
No, because Lambda refuses roles with administrator permissions
Yes: pass a powerful role to a new function and let an event source such as a DynamoDB stream trigger it
blocks.explain: This is Rhino's method 16: an event source mapping invokes the function without the attacker calling InvokeFunction. The fix is scoping PassRole by resource and iam:PassedToService, not removing one invoke permission.

blocks.question: Which change most directly closes Rhino's method 2, rolling a policy back with `iam:SetDefaultPolicyVersion`?
options: Turning on MFA for the user
Adding a permissions boundary that allows iam:*
Deleting old, broader policy versions and not granting SetDefaultPolicyVersion on policies the principal holds
Renaming the policy
blocks.explain: The impact of method 2 depends on what the inactive versions allow, so delete stale broad versions and do not let principals choose the default version of their own policies. A boundary allowing iam:* limits nothing here. CloudGoat's iam_privesc_by_rollback scenario lets you practise spotting this.

lessons.title: Graphing attack paths: role chains, PMapper and Access Analyzer

blocks.md:
Real escalations rarely take one step. An intern's user may assume a CI reader role; that role may pass a role to a Lambda function; the function's role may assume a deployer role; the deployer may attach a policy to itself. No single policy in that chain looks like an administrator. Together, they are one.

Two IAM terms first. **Role chaining** is, in AWS's words, "when you use a role to assume a second role". AWS limits a chained session to a maximum of one hour, regardless of the roles' own settings. An **attack path** is a sequence of such steps from a starting principal to something valuable. Finding them by reading policies one at a time does not scale; finding them is a graph search.

**The model.** Make every user and role a **node**. Draw a directed **edge** from A to B whenever A can become B, or act with B's permissions: B's trust policy lets A assume it; A can pass B to compute A controls; A can create credentials for B; A can edit B's policies or trust. Then "can the intern become an administrator?" is a reachability question, answered by breadth-first search (BFS: explore all one-step neighbours, then all two-step ones, and so on).

The code below does exactly that on a toy account. Its edges are written by hand; real tools derive them from every policy in the account.

blocks.title: Breadth-first search for a path to admin

scenes.caption: Each key lists the principals that node can become, and why. user/analyst has no edges at all.
BFS starts at user/intern with an empty path, then follows its only edge: the CI reader role's trust policy lets the intern assume it.
From ci-reader, PassRole plus CreateFunction reaches the lambda-ops role; from there role chaining reaches the deployer.
The deployer can attach a policy to itself, which is administrator. The search returns the four steps it took.
scenes.output:
user/intern can reach admin
   role/ci-reader   via sts:AssumeRole (trust policy)
   role/lambda-ops  via iam:PassRole + lambda:CreateFunction
   role/deployer    via sts:AssumeRole (role chaining)
   ADMIN            via iam:AttachRolePolicy on itself

scenes.caption: user/analyst has no outgoing edges, so the queue empties and the function returns None.
scenes.output:
user/intern can reach admin
   role/ci-reader   via sts:AssumeRole (trust policy)
   role/lambda-ops  via iam:PassRole + lambda:CreateFunction
   role/deployer    via sts:AssumeRole (role chaining)
   ADMIN            via iam:AttachRolePolicy on itself
user/analyst has no path to admin

blocks.title: Cutting one edge breaks the whole path

scenes.caption: The same toy account as a graph. Every edge is individually reasonable; the path through all of them is an intern becoming administrator.
Scope ci-reader's PassRole to app roles passed only to Lambda (lesson 6). The edge to lambda-ops disappears.
Nothing downstream changed, yet the intern can no longer reach admin. Defenders fix paths at their cheapest edge, not by rewriting every role.

blocks.md:
**Tools that build the graph for you** (use them only on accounts you own or are authorised to test):

- **PMapper** (Principal Mapper), from the security consultancy NCC Group and its author Erik Steringer, "models the different IAM Users and Roles in an account as a directed graph", which "enables checks for privilege escalation and for alternate paths": for example, a user who cannot read an S3 object "but could launch an EC2 instance that can read the S3 object".
- **Cloudsplaining**, from Salesforce, scans policies for least-privilege violations and groups risky actions as privilege escalation, resource exposure, data exfiltration, infrastructure modification and credentials exposure, in an HTML report.
- **pathfinding.cloud**, created and curated by Seth Art at Datadog, a monitoring and security company, documents cloud IAM escalation paths with detection notes and browser labs.

Defenders read their output as a to-do list: each path ends at an edge you can remove.

blocks.code:
# Build the graph for one account (read-only IAM access is enough)
pmapper --profile audit graph create

# Who can create IAM users, directly or through another principal?
pmapper --profile audit query 'who can do iam:CreateUser'

# Every privilege escalation path, skipping principals that are already admins
pmapper --account 111122223333 query -s 'preset privesc *'

# Draw admins, escalation paths and inter-principal access as an SVG
pmapper --account 111122223333 visualize --filetype svg
blocks.caption: Commands from PMapper's README with placeholder profile and account. Each result names the principal, the target and the edge to fix. PMapper has had no code changes since 2022, so it misses newer policy types such as RCPs; cross-check with Access Analyzer.

blocks.md:
**AWS's own analysis.** IAM Access Analyzer produces three kinds of findings. **External access** findings flag resource policies that grant access to principals outside your **zone of trust** (the organization or account you chose). **Internal access** findings report "a possible access path between an IAM role or user within your organization and your specified resources", computed with automated reasoning over all the policies. **Unused access** findings list roles not used in the usage window, credentials not used, and permissions unused in that window. Internal and unused access analysis are charged (per resource monitored and per role or user analyzed); external access findings are free. Unused permissions are the cheapest edges to remove: nobody will notice they are gone.

Commercial **CNAPP** tools (cloud-native application protection platforms, lesson 13) build the same kind of graph across clouds. Microsoft's Defender for Cloud, for instance, describes attack path analysis that finds "attack paths that start outside your organization and lead to critical targets".

Least privilege is a property of the graph, not of one policy. Ask "who can reach this role or this data, through any chain?", fix the cheapest edge on each path, and rerun the analysis after every IAM change.

blocks.question: A role is reached through role chaining and the caller requests a session of 4 hours (DurationSeconds 14400). What happens?
options: The request fails, because chained sessions are limited to one hour
The session lasts 4 hours if the role's maximum session duration allows it
The session is silently capped at 12 hours
Role chaining is not allowed at all
blocks.explain: AWS documents that role chaining limits the session to a maximum of one hour regardless of the roles' maximum session duration, and that asking for more than an hour with role chaining makes the operation fail.

blocks.question: PMapper reports that a CI role can reach admin in three hops. Which response best fits the graph view?
options: Delete every role on the path and recreate them
Add MFA to the CI role
Ignore it, because each individual policy looks narrow
Remove or scope the cheapest edge on the path, such as an unused PassRole, then rerun the query to confirm no path remains
blocks.explain: A path disappears when any one edge does, so fix the edge that is cheapest to remove (often an unused or over-broad permission) and verify with a new query. MFA does not apply to a role used by a pipeline.

lessons.title: Cross-account trust and the confused deputy

blocks.md:
The name comes from a 1988 paper by Norm Hardy, a computer scientist, about events some eleven years earlier at Tymshare, a commercial time-sharing company. A Tymshare compiler, (SYSX)FORT, had a special licence to write files in its own home directory, so it could record usage statistics. A user who knew the name of the billing file in that directory gave it to the compiler as the place to write debugging output. The operating system saw that the compiler had the licence and let it overwrite the billing file.

The compiler was a **deputy**: a program acting for someone else while holding authority of its own. It was **confused** because it used its own authority on a request from a user who had none. Hardy's point: the compiler's code was correct; it became wrong when it was given authority that callers could steer.

**The cloud version** is AWS's Example Corp scenario. Example Corp is a vendor that monitors AWS costs for many customers. Each customer creates a role whose trust policy trusts Example Corp's account, and hands Example Corp the role's ARN. Example Corp's software assumes each customer's role to read their bills.

A role ARN is not a secret. Suppose another Example Corp customer, Mallory, learns or guesses your role's ARN and registers it as their own. When Example Corp runs Mallory's job, it assumes **your** role, with its own perfectly valid credentials, and shows Mallory your data. Example Corp is now the confused deputy: its authority (being trusted by your role) was steered by someone who has none.

blocks.title: Example Corp as a confused deputy, then with an external ID

scenes.caption: Mallory registers with the vendor and supplies your role's ARN instead of their own. The vendor has no way to tell the ARN is not Mallory's.
The vendor assumes the role with its own account's credentials. Your trust policy only checks the vendor's account, so STS says yes.
The vendor reads your account and shows the result to Mallory, who never held any permission of their own.
Fixed: your trust policy now requires ExternalId 12345, the ID the vendor assigned you. For Mallory's job, the vendor always sends Mallory's ID, 67890.
The condition fails and STS refuses. Mallory cannot change the external ID the vendor sends, so knowing your ARN is no longer enough.

blocks.caption:
A model of the trust check, not AWS's code. Output:
old trust: job for you      credentials for YOUR account
old trust: job for mallory  credentials for YOUR account
new trust: job for you      credentials for YOUR account
new trust: job for mallory  AccessDenied

blocks.md:
**The external ID**, precisely, from AWS's documentation:

- It is a value in the role's trust policy, checked through the condition key `sts:ExternalId`. Its "primary function" is to prevent the confused deputy problem.
- It must be **unique per customer and controlled by the vendor**: "you get it from Example Corp and you don't come up with it on your own". The vendor always sends the ID of the customer whose job it is running.
- It is **not a secret**: "The external ID for a role can be seen by anyone with permission to view the role." Its strength comes from the vendor controlling which ID goes with which job.
- Vendors should test each customer's role both with and without the correct ID, and refuse to store a role ARN that can be assumed without it.

The trust policy below is the customer's side.

blocks.caption: The vendor's account is the principal (the root ARN here means the account, not its root user). Real external IDs are long unique values such as GUIDs; 12345 follows AWS's simplified example.

blocks.md:
**Cross-service confused deputy.** AWS services act as deputies too. A bucket policy that lets the service principal `cloudtrail.amazonaws.com` write logs, with no condition, accepts CloudTrail logs from any account whose admin knows the bucket name. AWS's fix is a set of condition keys that say on whose behalf the service is acting: `aws:SourceArn` (a specific resource, such as your trail), `aws:SourceAccount`, `aws:SourceOrgID` and `aws:SourceOrgPaths`. AWS recommends using them "wherever an AWS service principal is granted permission to access one of your resources".

A serverless case: when S3 invokes a Lambda function, the source is a bucket whose ARN contains no account ID. The Lambda documentation warns you "could delete a bucket and another account could create a bucket with the same name", so the function's resource policy should also require `aws:SourceAccount`. Inside your organization, resource policies can grant access by `aws:PrincipalOrgID` instead of listing accounts, so a new account joins the trust automatically and outsiders never do.

blocks.caption: Pattern from AWS's cross-service confused deputy example: the service principal may write only on behalf of one named trail. Without the SourceArn test, anyone's CloudTrail could deliver into this bucket.

blocks.md:
**Defender view.**

- *Find:* IAM Access Analyzer's external access findings include roles whose trust policies let principals outside your zone of trust assume them. Review every such role: is the account a known vendor, and does the trust require an external ID?
- *Prevent:* require `sts:ExternalId` for every third-party role, add source conditions to every service principal grant, and back them with an organization-wide RCP; AWS's identity perimeter example has a statement for exactly this, keyed on `aws:SourceOrgID`.
- *Detect:* `AssumeRole` calls on vendor roles in CloudTrail at unusual times, or from a vendor you have stopped using, mean the trust outlived the relationship. Remove trust when a contract ends.

blocks.question: A vendor asks you to create a cross-account role and suggests you choose the external ID yourself, "any value you like". What is wrong with that?
options: Nothing; any external ID works the same
The external ID must be generated and controlled by the vendor, unique per customer, or another customer could register the same value
External IDs must be kept secret, so the vendor should never see it
External IDs only work for roles in the same account
blocks.explain: AWS says the external ID must be unique among the vendor's customers and controlled by the vendor, not the customer. If customers choose it, two could pick the same value and the deputy is confused again. AWS also says the ID is not a secret.

blocks.question: A Lambda function's resource policy lets `s3.amazonaws.com` invoke it with `aws:SourceArn` set to `arn:aws:s3:::uploads-bucket`, and nothing else. The bucket is later deleted. What risk does AWS's documentation describe?
options: Another account could create a bucket with the same name and trigger the function; adding aws:SourceAccount closes this
None, because bucket ARNs are unique forever
The function is deleted automatically with the bucket
S3 will start invoking the function with administrator rights
blocks.explain: Bucket ARNs contain no account ID, and a deleted bucket name can be created again by someone else. The Lambda docs recommend aws:SourceAccount (the --source-account option) for S3 triggers.

lessons.title: Serverless: execution roles, event injection and function secrets

blocks.md:
A photo app resizes every uploaded image with a small function. There is no server to patch and nothing runs between uploads. It is tempting to conclude there is nothing to secure. But the function still runs code, holds a role, is triggered by data that strangers control, and needs a database password.

**Serverless** means you hand the provider code and it runs the servers; **FaaS** (function as a service) is the form where you hand over single functions, such as AWS Lambda, Azure Functions and Google's Cloud Run functions. In shared responsibility terms (the cloud security and IAM course), this moves the line further toward the provider than IaaS. Microsoft's shared responsibility page lists Azure Functions among PaaS services, and says that whatever the service model you always keep your data, endpoints, accounts and access management. For AWS Lambda's managed runtimes, "Lambda takes on the operational burden of patching the runtime versions" by default; functions deployed as container images must be rebuilt from updated base images by you.

blocks.title: Who secures what (0 provider, 0.5 shared, 1 customer)

scenes.caption: Rows from Microsoft's shared responsibility page. Moving right, the provider takes over more layers. FaaS such as Lambda sits near PaaS: no operating system for you to patch.
The bottom two rows never move: in every model the customer owns accounts, access control and data. That is where serverless breaches happen.
Applications are shared in PaaS and SaaS: the provider runs the stack, you own configuration, code security and access controls. A function's code is yours.

blocks.md:
**The execution role.** A Lambda function's **execution role** is an IAM role that "grants the function permission to access AWS services and resources", and "Lambda automatically assumes your execution role when you invoke your function". The temporary credentials are handed to your code as environment variables named `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` and `AWS_SESSION_TOKEN`. So any code that runs inside the function, including code an attacker injects, holds the role.

When the console creates a role for you it attaches only `AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole`, which allows writing logs. The risky pattern is the opposite: one broad role shared by every function "to keep things simple". Give each function its own role with only the actions and resources it uses, and remember lesson 6: `lambda:UpdateFunctionCode` on a function is a path to its role.

**Who may invoke it.** A function also has a **resource-based policy** saying who can call it. For AWS services, add source conditions (lesson 8): for an S3 trigger, `aws:SourceAccount` as well as the bucket ARN. A **function URL** gives a function its own HTTPS endpoint, with an `AuthType` of either `AWS_IAM` (callers must be signed IAM principals) or `NONE`, where "Lambda doesn't perform any authentication before invoking your function". `NONE` suits a public webhook, but then the code is the only control. IAM Access Analyzer flags functions with public or cross-account access, at no charge.

**Event injection.** The OWASP Top 10: Serverless Interpretation (2018, from OWASP, the Open Worldwide Application Security Project) points out that functions are triggered by storage events, streams, database changes and notifications, so "we should no longer consider input coming directly from the API calls as the sole attack surface", and if a function is triggered by email or a database "there is nowhere to put a Firewall". An S3 object key is chosen by whoever uploads the file.

blocks.title: Command injection through an S3 object key
blocks.code:
import subprocess
from urllib.parse import unquote_plus

def handler(event, context):
    # Triggered by an S3 upload. Whoever uploads chooses the object key.
    key = unquote_plus(event["Records"][0]["s3"]["object"]["key"])
    # BUG: the key is pasted into a shell command line
    out = subprocess.run(f"echo resizing {key}", shell=True,
                         capture_output=True, text=True)
    return out.stdout

# S3 sends the key URL-encoded: this is "cat.jpg; echo INJECTED"
event = {"Records": [{"s3": {"object": {"key": "cat.jpg%3B+echo+INJECTED"}}}]}
print(handler(event, None), end="")

scenes.caption: An upload triggers the function. The event carries the object key, URL-encoded as S3 always sends it, and the uploader chose that name.
unquote_plus decodes it. The key now contains a semicolon, which a shell reads as "end of command, start the next one".
The bug: the key is pasted into a command string run with shell=True. The shell sees two commands.
Both commands ran. Here the second one is a harmless echo, but it runs with the function's role credentials in its environment.

blocks.code:
import re
import subprocess
from urllib.parse import unquote_plus

SAFE_KEY = re.compile(r"(?!.*\.\.)[A-Za-z0-9_][A-Za-z0-9/_.-]{0,199}\.jpg")

def handler(event, context):
    key = unquote_plus(event["Records"][0]["s3"]["object"]["key"])
    if not SAFE_KEY.fullmatch(key):          # allow list, not a block list
        return f"rejected key {key!r}\n"
    # No shell: the key is one argument and is never parsed as a command
    out = subprocess.run(["echo", "resizing", key],
                         capture_output=True, text=True)
    return out.stdout

for k in ["cat.jpg%3B+echo+INJECTED", "uploads/cat.jpg"]:
    event = {"Records": [{"s3": {"object": {"key": k}}}]}
    print(handler(event, None), end="")
blocks.caption:
FIXED. Output:
rejected key 'cat.jpg; echo INJECTED'
resizing uploads/cat.jpg

blocks.md: **Why the fix works.** Passing a list to `subprocess.run` without `shell=True` runs the program directly: the key is a single argument and no shell ever parses it, so `;`, `|` or `$()` mean nothing. The allow-list regular expression rejects any key that is not a plain path ending in `.jpg`, including keys that start with a dash (which a tool would read as an option) or contain `..`, which also protects the image tool from odd file names. You met both rules in the injection attacks course; serverless only changes where the input comes from. A third layer limits the damage if a bug remains: the execution role can read the uploads bucket and write the thumbnails bucket, nothing else. OWASP's guidance says the same: "the impact of a successful injection attack will lean on the permission the vulnerable function has".

**Secrets in functions.** Lambda environment variables are encrypted at rest with a KMS key, by default an AWS managed key. They are still readable configuration: `GetFunctionConfiguration` returns them (AWS notes they are omitted from CloudTrail logs), so anyone allowed to read the function's configuration can read them. AWS's docs say that with a customer managed key, "only users in your account with access to the KMS key can view or manage environment variables". AWS recommends Secrets Manager "instead of environment variables" for database credentials, API keys and tokens; the function fetches the secret at run time with its role, for example through the AWS Parameters and Secrets Lambda extension.

**Other clouds.** In Google Cloud, Compute Engine and services built on it use the Compute Engine default service account unless you attach another, and Google warns that default service accounts may hold the broad Editor role (lesson 12). Azure Functions use managed identities, covered in the cloud security and IAM course.

**Defender view.**

- *Prevent:* one least-privilege role per function, source conditions on every resource policy, `AWS_IAM` function URLs unless public by design, no secrets in environment variables, input validation for every event source.
- *Detect:* in CloudTrail, `UpdateFunctionCode`, `UpdateFunctionConfiguration`, `AddPermission` and `CreateFunctionUrlConfig` from anyone other than your deployment pipeline. GuardDuty Lambda Protection monitors Lambda network activity logs and raises findings when traffic suggests malicious code in a function. Access Analyzer flags functions that became public.
- *Respond:* redeploy the function from source, revoke the execution role's sessions (the cloud security and IAM course showed how) and rotate any secret the function could read.

Serverless removes servers, not responsibility. A function is code plus a role plus its triggers: validate every event as untrusted input, give each function only the role it needs, and keep secrets in a secret store rather than in configuration.

blocks.question: An attacker achieves code execution in a Lambda function through an injection bug. What can their code do with AWS?
options: Nothing, because Lambda functions have no credentials
Only read the function's own logs
Anything the function's execution role allows, using the credentials Lambda places in the function's environment
Act as the AWS account's root user
blocks.explain: Lambda assumes the execution role on invocation and exposes its temporary credentials as environment variables. The role's permissions set the blast radius, which is why each function needs its own least-privilege role.

blocks.question: A function URL is configured with AuthType NONE and a resource-based policy allowing public invocation. Which statement is true?
options: Lambda still checks for an IAM signature before running the code
Anyone on the internet can invoke it, so the function's code is the only control
AuthType NONE only allows calls from inside the same VPC
IAM Access Analyzer cannot see function URLs
blocks.explain: With NONE, AWS says Lambda performs no authentication before invoking the function; the resource policy must allow public access, and then anyone can call it. Access Analyzer reports public and cross-account access to functions.

blocks.question: A team stores the database password as a Lambda environment variable, encrypted with the default AWS managed key. Who can read it?
options: Only the function itself
Nobody, because environment variables are encrypted
Only the AWS account root user
Any principal allowed to read the function's configuration, since GetFunctionConfiguration returns the variables
blocks.explain: Encryption at rest does not hide values from callers allowed to read the configuration. AWS recommends Secrets Manager for credentials; a customer managed key at least restricts viewing to users who can use that key.

lessons.title: Human access: LastPass 2022, Identity Center and break-glass

blocks.md:
LastPass, a password manager company, disclosed two linked incidents in 2022. In the first, a software engineer's corporate laptop was compromised, and the attacker took source code (14 of 200 repositories) and internal scripts that held secrets. LastPass's March 2023 update says the threat actor then "pivoted", and from August 12 to October 26, 2022 worked on the cloud storage environment.

The backups in Amazon S3 were encrypted, and the attacker needed both AWS access keys and LastPass's own decryption keys, which were kept in only two places. One was a restricted set of shared folders in a LastPass vault used by DevOps engineers. So the attacker targeted "one of the four DevOps engineers who had access to the decryption keys".

How, in LastPass's words: by "targeting the DevOps engineer's home computer and exploiting a vulnerable third-party media software package, which enabled remote code execution capability and allowed the threat actor to implant keylogger malware". The keylogger captured the engineer's master password "as it was entered, after the employee authenticated with MFA". The attacker then exported the vault entries and shared folders, which "contained encrypted secure notes with access and decryption keys needed to access the AWS S3 LastPass production backups".

Detection was hard because the actions used valid credentials of a senior engineer, which "made it difficult for investigators to differentiate between threat actor activity and ongoing legitimate activity". In the end, LastPass says, "AWS GuardDuty Alerts informed us of anomalous behavior as the threat actor attempted to use Cloud Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles to perform unauthorized activity."

blocks.title: LastPass incident 2, and where each control would cut the chain

nodes.label:
Secure notes: AWS keys
and decryption keys

scenes.caption: The chain as LastPass described it: a home computer, a keylogger, the engineer's vault, long-lived AWS keys and decryption keys in secure notes, then the S3 backups.
Endpoint: Microsoft lists endpoints among the responsibilities the customer always keeps. A personal machine with vulnerable software could reach corporate secrets.
Long-lived keys: access keys stored as notes work for whoever copies them. Identity Center sessions are temporary and require a fresh sign-in with MFA.
With roles from Identity Center instead of stored keys, the note holds nothing reusable, and an SCP can forbid creating IAM users and access keys at all.

labels.keys:
Nothing to steal:
sessions from Identity Center

scenes.caption: A network perimeter (lesson 4) adds a last check: even valid keys fail from outside expected networks. LastPass later applied tighter IP restrictions.

blocks.md:
What LastPass changed afterwards includes, among other steps: they "enabled a policy that prevents the creation and use of long-lived development IAM users", rotated production service IAM user keys and applied tighter IP restrictions, deleted obsolete IAM users, and enabled "Microsoft's conditional access PIN-matching multifactor authentication".

The architecture lesson is about **workforce identity**: how people, not workloads, get into cloud accounts. Notice what MFA did and did not do here. The engineer did use MFA; the keylogger stole a password typed after it, and the real prize was not a session but long-lived keys stored as text. MFA protects sign-ins. It cannot protect a credential that never needs a sign-in. The fix is to stop having such credentials.

**AWS IAM Identity Center** (named AWS Single Sign-On until July 26, 2022) connects your workforce directory, an external identity provider (IdP) such as Entra ID or Okta or its own user store, to every account in the organization.

Access is granted with **permission sets**: "a template that you create and maintain that defines a collection" of policies. When you assign a permission set to a group for an account, Identity Center "creates corresponding IAM Identity Center-controlled IAM roles in each account" and lets the assigned users assume them through the AWS access portal or CLI. Sessions last 1 hour by default (1 to 12 hours allowed). Nobody holds an access key.

Identity Center's own directory has MFA on by default; with an external IdP, the IdP enforces MFA. AWS recommends **phishing-resistant MFA** "such as passkeys and security keys", FIDO-based authenticators that resist "phishing, man-in-the-middle, and replay attacks" (FIDO and passkeys were covered in the authentication and identity attacks course).

blocks.title: An engineer reaches the Prod account with no stored key

scenes.caption: The engineer opens the AWS access portal, which sends them to the company IdP to sign in.
The IdP checks the password and a passkey. The passkey signs a challenge bound to the real site, so a look-alike page gets nothing usable.
Identity Center shows only the accounts and permission sets assigned to the engineer's groups. They choose ReadOnly in Prod.
Identity Center returns temporary credentials for the role it created in Prod for that permission set. The engineer calls Prod with them until the session expires.
Nothing persistent was issued. When the engineer leaves, disabling them in the IdP ends every future session in every account.

blocks.md:
**Root and break-glass.** With **centralized root access**, the organization deletes member accounts' root credentials; new accounts "have no root user credentials by default", and root-only tasks run from the management account or a delegated administrator.

**Break-glass** access is the planned, emergency-only way in when normal sign-in fails.
