AWS recommends an emergency configuration that federates designated users directly into accounts if Identity Center is disrupted, set up and tested in advance. Microsoft's guidance for Entra ID: two or more cloud-only emergency accounts, passwordless phishing-resistant sign-in (passkey or certificate), excluded from Conditional Access policies (Entra's sign-in rules that block or demand extra checks) that could block them, an alert on every use, and a functional check at least every 90 days. For everyday admin rights, Entra **PIM** (Privileged Identity Management) makes roles "eligible" rather than permanent: users activate them just in time, for a limited period, with MFA, justification or approval.

blocks.caption: Simplified from AWS's example SCP denying critical IAM user actions. Attached to the Workloads and Sandbox OUs, it makes Identity Center roles the only way in for people. LastPass adopted a policy with the same goal for its development environment.

blocks.md: "We have MFA, so stolen passwords do not matter" is the misconception LastPass disproves. MFA protects the sign-in it guards. Long-lived access keys, keys stored in notes and anything readable from an already compromised device are outside its reach. Remove standing credentials, require phishing-resistant MFA, and treat engineer endpoints as part of production.

blocks.question: According to LastPass, at what point did the keylogger capture the DevOps engineer's master password?
options: Before the engineer completed MFA, so MFA would have stopped it
From a phishing page imitating the vault
As it was typed, after the engineer had authenticated with MFA
From a database backup in S3
blocks.explain: LastPass says the keylogger captured the master password as it was entered, after the employee authenticated with MFA. That is why the durable fix is removing long-lived secrets and hardening endpoints, not only adding factors.

blocks.question: An organization moves all engineers to IAM Identity Center and attaches the NoLongLivedHumanCredentials SCP to every workload OU. A break-glass role is named in the exemption. What still needs to be in place?
options: A tested emergency path that does not depend on Identity Center, with alerts on every use
Nothing; break-glass access works automatically
Access keys for every engineer as a backup
Turning off MFA for the break-glass role so it is always usable
blocks.explain: AWS recommends setting up and periodically testing emergency access that works if Identity Center is disrupted, and Microsoft recommends alerting on every use of emergency accounts. Spare access keys would recreate the LastPass problem; emergency accounts should use strong, phishing-resistant authentication.

lessons.title: Azure in depth: role assignments, Run Command and PIM

blocks.md:
A developer has the **Contributor** role on a subscription. Can they make themselves **Owner**? Microsoft's role definitions answer directly. Contributor "grants full access to manage all resources, but does not allow you to assign roles in Azure RBAC". Owner "grants full access to manage all resources, including the ability to assign roles in Azure RBAC". The difference is one family of permissions: writing role assignments, `Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write`.

So in Azure, the AWS question "who can edit IAM policies?" becomes "who can write role assignments, and at which scope?" Roles that can: Owner, **User Access Administrator** ("Lets you manage user access to Azure resources") and **Role Based Access Control Administrator**. At the tenant level, a Global Administrator can elevate to User Access Administrator over every subscription, as the cloud security and IAM course showed. Entra ID adds another: Microsoft warns an Application Administrator can "add credentials to an application, and use those credentials to impersonate the application's identity".

Microsoft lists the problems with handing out Owner or User Access Administrator just so someone can grant access. The delegate "can assign any role to any user within their scope, including themselves", and can assign Owner or User Access Administrator to others, who can do the same.

The safer pattern is **delegating role assignment management with conditions**: give the Role Based Access Control Administrator role with a condition that limits which roles it may assign and to which principals. Microsoft's example: Dara may add or remove only Backup Contributor or Backup Reader assignments, only for the Marketing and Sales groups; any other assignment fails. It is the Azure counterpart of the AWS permissions boundary trick in lesson 6: the right to grant, without the right to grant yourself everything.

blocks.title: Three Azure routes to more privilege

nodes.label:
User Access Admin
or RBAC Admin

scenes.caption: Three starting points a defender should recognise. Each ends with control over more of the subscription than the starting role suggests.
Route 1: anyone who can write role assignments at a scope can assign Owner to themselves at that scope.
Route 2: Virtual Machine Contributor can use Run Command. Scripts run on the VM as System on Windows, so the caller's code now runs inside the VM.
Code on the VM can ask the local metadata endpoint for the VM's managed identity token. If that identity holds Contributor, so does whoever ran the command.
Route 3: a Global Administrator elevates to User Access Administrator at the root of all subscriptions, then follows route 1.
Defences: PIM makes these roles eligible, not standing; conditions limit what delegates may assign; privileged identities stay off VMs that many people can run commands on.

blocks.md:
**Run Command and managed identities, precisely.** Microsoft's documentation says running a command "requires the `Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/runCommand/action` permission. The Virtual Machine Contributor role and higher levels have this permission", and that scripts run as System on Windows. A **managed identity** (the cloud security and IAM course) is how code on a VM gets Azure credentials without storing any: the code asks the Azure **Instance Metadata Service** at 169.254.169.254 for a token, as below. That convenience is also the risk. Any code that runs on the VM, whether a bug, a malicious package or a Run Command script, can ask for the same token.

This is Azure's version of AWS's class 5 escalation in lesson 6: control over compute is control over the identity attached to it. Google gives the same warning about service accounts (lesson 12): do not attach a privileged identity to a machine that less trusted people or code can run on.

blocks.code:
# How legitimate code on an Azure VM gets its managed identity's token.
# The header proves the call came from the VM itself, not through a proxy.
GET http://169.254.169.254/metadata/identity/oauth2/token?api-version=2018-02-01&resource=https://management.azure.com/ HTTP/1.1
Metadata: true

# Defender's reading: anyone who can run code on this VM can make this call.
# Who holds runCommand/action on the VM = who can act as its identity.
blocks.caption: The request is from Microsoft's documentation for acquiring a managed identity token on a VM. Microsoft says the required Metadata header is "a mitigation against server side request forgery (SSRF) attacks", a role like IMDSv2's session token in AWS.

blocks.md:
**Privileged Identity Management (PIM)** is Azure's main control for standing privilege: "just-in-time privileged access", "time-bound access" and the option to "require approval to activate privileged roles". An **eligible** assignment does nothing until the user activates it, with MFA, a justification or an approver. Making Owner and User Access Administrator eligible rather than active removes most standing privilege.

**Defender for Cloud** is Microsoft's **CNAPP** (lesson 13), combining posture management, workload protection and entitlement analysis. Its attack path analysis looks for paths "that start outside your organization and lead to critical targets", the Azure version of the graph search in lesson 7.

**Detection.** In the Azure activity log, alert on role assignment writes for Owner, User Access Administrator or Role Based Access Control Administrator and on Run Command against VMs with privileged identities; in Entra's audit log, on PIM activations of the most powerful roles.

In Azure, the keys to escalation are writing role assignments and running code where a privileged identity lives. Make powerful roles eligible through PIM, delegate assignments with conditions instead of Owner, and treat Virtual Machine Contributor on a VM as equal to that VM's managed identity.

blocks.question: A user holds Virtual Machine Contributor on a VM. The VM has a system-assigned managed identity with Contributor on the subscription. What is the realistic effective privilege of the user?
options: Only managing that VM's configuration
Owner on the subscription
None, because managed identity tokens cannot be requested from Run Command scripts
Contributor on the subscription, because Run Command lets their code request the identity's token on the VM
blocks.explain: Virtual Machine Contributor includes runCommand/action, so the user's script runs on the VM and can ask the metadata endpoint for the identity's token. Contributor still cannot assign roles, so it is not Owner.

blocks.question: A team lead needs to let a colleague grant the AcrPull role to the team's managed identities, and nothing else. What does Microsoft recommend instead of giving them User Access Administrator?
options: Give them Owner, since it is the same thing
Role Based Access Control Administrator with a condition limiting which roles and principals they can assign
Contributor, which can assign AcrPull
A Global Administrator account for emergencies
blocks.explain: Microsoft's guidance is to delegate role assignment management with conditions on the Role Based Access Control Administrator role. User Access Administrator lets the delegate assign any role, even to themselves; Contributor cannot assign roles at all.

lessons.title: Google Cloud in depth: service accounts, actAs and impersonation

blocks.md:
In Google Cloud, almost every escalation question is a question about **service accounts**, the identities that workloads use. Two permissions matter most, and each has an AWS twin you already know:

- **Attaching** a service account to a resource, such as a VM or a Cloud Run service, needs `iam.serviceAccounts.actAs`, included in the **Service Account User** role (`roles/iam.serviceAccountUser`). Code on that resource can then get the service account's credentials. This is AWS's `iam:PassRole` (lesson 6, class 4).
- **Impersonating** a service account directly, by minting short-lived credentials for it, needs the **Service Account Token Creator** role (`roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator`), which "lets principals create short-lived credentials for a service account". This is AWS's `sts:AssumeRole`.

Google notes some services once skipped the `actAs` check, and "this legacy behavior still exists for some organizations". Also guard `resourcemanager.projects.setIamPolicy` (grant yourself any role: class 1) and `iam.serviceAccountKeys.create` (a long-lived key: class 2).

**The default service account problem.** Compute Engine, and services built on it, run as the Compute Engine default service account unless you choose another. Google says it "might automatically be granted the Editor role on your project", and Editor "lets the service account create and delete resources for most Google Cloud services". Google "strongly" recommends disabling the automatic grant with the constraint `iam.automaticIamGrantsForDefaultServiceAccounts`, which is enforced by default for organizations created on or after May 3, 2024 (lesson 5).

**Granting at the wrong level.** Google's best practices warn that granting Token Creator on a whole project means "the user can impersonate any service account in the Google Cloud project", which "implies that the user can potentially gain access to all resources that those service accounts can access, including resources outside that Google Cloud project". Their advice: manage access to each service account individually, not at the project or folder level.

blocks.title: Two Google Cloud routes from a narrow role to Editor

scenes.caption: A developer holds a narrow role on the project plus Service Account User on the default compute service account, which (in an older organization) has Editor.
Route 1, attach: the developer creates a VM running as the default service account. actAs is exactly the permission that allows this.
Code on the VM asks the metadata server for the attached account's credentials and acts with Editor on the project.
Route 2, impersonate: Token Creator granted on the whole project lets the developer mint tokens for every service account in it, including ones with access elsewhere.
Fixes: no Editor on default service accounts, a dedicated least-privilege account per workload, and actAs or Token Creator granted on one service account, never the project.

blocks.code:
# Who may use (actAs) or impersonate this service account?
gcloud iam service-accounts get-iam-policy \
    app-runner@shop-prod.iam.gserviceaccount.com

# Project-level bindings: look for roles/iam.serviceAccountUser,
# roles/iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator, and roles/editor on default accounts
gcloud projects get-iam-policy shop-prod --format=json

# Is the baseline in force for this project?
gcloud org-policies describe iam.automaticIamGrantsForDefaultServiceAccounts \
    --project=shop-prod --effective
blocks.caption: Read-only audit commands with placeholder names. A binding of Service Account User or Token Creator at project level is a finding: it applies to every service account in the project.

blocks.md:
**Defences, in order of payoff.**

1. Enforce lesson 5's baseline constraints on older organizations.
2. Give each workload its own service account with only the roles it needs, and grant Service Account User and Token Creator on that one account to the people or pipelines that deploy it.
3. Google's advice: don't run code from less protected sources on compute that has a privileged service account attached, because "processes running on that resource can use the metadata server" to get its credentials.
4. Use **IAM deny policies** for permissions nobody should use regardless of roles, and **VPC Service Controls** around sensitive data (lesson 5).

**Detection.** Admin Activity audit logs, which are always written, record IAM policy changes such as new Token Creator or Service Account User bindings. Google's **lateral movement insights** point out a service account in one project that has permission to impersonate a service account in another. **Security Command Center**, Google's "cloud-based risk management solution", gathers posture findings.

Google Cloud escalation runs through service accounts: actAs is PassRole and Token Creator is AssumeRole. Remove Editor from default service accounts, grant both roles on individual service accounts only, and never attach a privileged service account to compute that less trusted code can run on.

blocks.question: Why does Google advise against granting the Service Account Token Creator role at the project level?
options: The user can impersonate every service account in the project and reach whatever those accounts can access, even outside the project
It is billed per project
It disables Admin Activity audit logs
Project-level roles expire after 15 minutes
blocks.explain: Google's best practices say project-level Token Creator lets the user impersonate any service account in the project, potentially reaching all resources those accounts can access, including outside the project.

blocks.question: Which AWS permission is the closest equivalent of Google Cloud's iam.serviceAccounts.actAs?
options: sts:GetCallerIdentity
s3:GetObject
iam:PassRole
organizations:LeaveOrganization
blocks.explain: actAs lets a principal attach a service account to a resource so that code running there uses its credentials, which is what iam:PassRole does for an AWS service. Impersonation through Token Creator is closer to sts:AssumeRole.

lessons.title: CSPM, CIEM and CNAPP, and a full architecture review

blocks.md:
A company with 300 AWS accounts and 40 Azure subscriptions cannot review every policy by hand. The cloud security and IAM course introduced **CSPM** (cloud security posture management: continuously comparing live configuration against rules). Three more names come up in every job posting:

- **CWPP** (cloud workload protection platform): protects the running workloads themselves; Microsoft's definition lists "virtual machines (VMs), containers, storage, databases, and serverless functions".
- **CIEM** (cloud infrastructure entitlement management; an entitlement is a granted right): analyses who can access what, the graph from lesson 7. Microsoft's Defender for Cloud describes CIEM as helping organizations "discover, assess, and manage identity and access risks across their multicloud environments".
- **CNAPP** (cloud-native application protection platform): Microsoft calls Defender for Cloud a CNAPP, "a unified solution that combines multiple cloud security tools to protect applications across their entire lifecycle", from code to runtime.

**What the tools do with all those findings.** A single misconfiguration rarely matters on its own. The findings worth waking up for are combinations that form a path: an internet-reachable function, plus an injection bug, plus an execution role that can read a sensitive bucket. That is lesson 9 plus lesson 7. Attack path analysis in CNAPP products, and open source graph tools, rank findings by whether they sit on such a path.

Open source and native options:

- **Prowler**, an open source tool that runs security and compliance checks across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud and Kubernetes.
- **AWS Security Hub CSPM**, which assesses accounts against standards such as AWS Foundational Security Best Practices, aggregated in the Security Tooling account (lesson 2).
- **Google Security Command Center**, and **Microsoft Defender for Cloud**, the native equivalents.

blocks.title: Review: one stolen developer key meets every layer of this course

scenes.caption: A developer's credential is phished. In the Code Spaces design this would be the end of the story. Follow it through the layers of the finished architecture.
Lesson 10: humans hold no access keys. The phished password alone fails the passkey check, and sessions from Identity Center expire within hours.
Lessons 3 to 5: if a session is stolen anyway, SCPs stop it creating users, leaving approved Regions or touching platform roles.
Lessons 6 to 9: path analysis has already removed the edges from the developer's role to admin, and functions run with narrow roles.
Lesson 4: the data perimeter blocks copying data to an outside account or using credentials from unexpected networks.
Lessons 1 and 2: every attempt lands in the Log Archive, and the last good copy of the data sits in a locked vault in another account.

blocks.md:
**An architecture review checklist** built from this course. For each organization (or tenant):

1. Accounts and OUs separate production, non-production, sandbox, logs, security tooling and backups; the management account has no workloads.
2. Deny-list SCPs (or Azure Policy and Google organization policy) block leaving the organization, unapproved Regions, IAM users and keys, changes to logging and platform roles; each has a tested exemption for break-glass.
3. A data perimeter: RCPs (or VPC Service Controls) keep outside identities away from your data, and SCPs keep your identities away from outside resources.
4. No principal can reach admin through PassRole, policy edits, trust edits or function code changes; verified with a graph tool after every IAM change.
5. Every third-party role requires an external ID; every service principal grant has a source condition.
6. Every function has its own least-privilege role and no secrets in environment variables.
7. People sign in through one IdP with phishing-resistant MFA; no standing admin roles; break-glass is tested and alerted.

**Where this sits in the CCSP.** The Certified Cloud Security Professional exam from ISC2, a nonprofit security certification body, has six domains. In the outline effective August 1, 2026, the average weights are: Cloud Concepts, Architecture and Design 17%; Cloud Data Security 20%; Cloud Platform and Infrastructure Security 17%; Cloud Application Security 16%; Cloud Security Operations 17%; Legal, Risk and Compliance 13%. This course mostly serves domains 1 and 3, with parts of 2 (perimeters, backups), 4 (serverless) and 5 (access, posture).

**Practise legally**, in accounts you own and can delete, or on platforms built for it:

- [CloudGoat](https://github.com/RhinoSecurityLabs/cloudgoat), Rhino Security Labs' "Vulnerable by Design" deployment tool: scenarios such as iam_privesc_by_rollback, iam_privesc_by_attachment, lambda_privesc and vulnerable_lambda map to lessons 6 and 9.
- [flAWS 2](http://flaws2.cloud/), by Scott Piper, with attacker and defender paths.
- [pathfinding.cloud](https://pathfinding.cloud/), browser labs for IAM escalation paths, no cloud account needed.

blocks.title: CCSP exam domains, average weight (outline effective August 1, 2026)

scenes.caption: ISC2's published weights for the six CCSP domains. Data security is the largest single domain; legal, risk and compliance the smallest.
The domains this course covers most deeply: architecture and design, and platform and infrastructure security, together about a third of the exam.

blocks.md: A good cloud architecture assumes one credential, one function or one account will fail, and makes sure that failure stays small: walls between accounts, guardrails nobody can lift, no hidden paths to admin, no standing human keys, logs and backups out of reach. Posture tools help you keep it that way; they do not design it for you.

blocks.question: A CNAPP reports 4,000 findings. Which one should a team fix first?
options: Detailed monitoring is disabled on 600 instances
An internet-reachable function with a known injection bug whose execution role can read the customer data bucket
Tags are missing on 1,200 resources
A sandbox account uses an older instance type
blocks.explain: Prioritise findings that form an attack path to sensitive data. The function combines exposure, a vulnerability and a privileged identity, which is exactly the toxic combination attack path analysis is built to surface.

blocks.question: Which of these is a CIEM capability rather than CSPM?
options: Checking that storage encryption is enabled
Scanning a container image for vulnerable packages
Checking that logging is turned on in every Region
Mapping which identities can reach which resources, including through chains of roles
blocks.explain: CIEM is about entitlements: who can access what. Encryption and logging checks are posture (CSPM); image scanning is workload protection (CWPP).
